instances.excerpt: A manufacturer must notify regulators and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. A mandatory recall is required when a model exceeds 12 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or sooner if a regulator determines an imminent serious risk warrants it.

parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a material risk to users or nearby people, and provide safety instructions and updates.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a material risk to users or nearby people, and provide safety instructions and updates.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a material risk to users or nearby people, and provide safety instructions and updates. Reports must include the model, incident date and circumstances, injuries or damage, and any response taken.

parameters.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C before market launch and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-recognized protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers shall submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to regulators and provide those results to customers who buy that model. The maximum allowed failure rate is 5%. A model exceeding 5% may not be newly placed on the market until corrective action is completed and a retest demonstrates a failure rate of 5% or less; the manufacturer must submit a corrective-action plan within 30 days and complete the retest within six months.

Manufacturers shall submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to regulators and provide those results to customers who buy that model. The maximum allowed failure rate is 5%. A model exceeding 5% may not be newly placed on the market until corrective action is completed and a retest demonstrates a failure rate of 5% or less; the manufacturer must submit a corrective-action plan within 30 days and complete the retest within six months.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C before market launch and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-recognized protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers shall submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to regulators and provide those results to customers who buy that model. The maximum allowed failure rate is 5%. A model exceeding 5% may not be newly placed on the market until corrective action is completed and a retest demonstrates a failure rate of 5% or less; the manufacturer must submit a corrective-action plan within 30 days and complete the retest within six months. Regulators may require additional protective measures for existing units based on the results.

parameters.quote: All new home battery systems placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers shall provide a secure, reliable shut-off capability and instructions for its use. Existing installed units that can practicably be retrofitted must be upgraded within six years of the standard’s effective date; units not compatible with retrofit must be disclosed to their owners and addressed through a regulator-approved safety plan.

parameters.quote: New home battery systems placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression beginning three years after the standard’s effective date. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and designed to limit fire propagation and protect occupants and nearby people.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery systems placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression beginning three years after the standard’s effective date. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and designed to limit fire propagation and protect occupants and nearby people.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery systems placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression beginning three years after the standard’s effective date. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and designed to limit fire propagation and protect occupants and nearby people. Manufacturers must document the system’s performance and maintenance requirements.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: For evidence-based discussion: Northwind recorded 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide last year; three thermal incidents were not reported to regulators. Hearth 10 had a 6.2% 55°C sustained-heat failure rate and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units. Remote shut-off is supported by 38% of our installed units; built-in suppression costs $42/unit. We can provide model-level test results to regulators confidentially, but do not agree to public disclosure of individual companies’ per-model failure rates.

judge_section_notes: The final rules adopt a strict 55°C/5% thermal-testing standard with per-model results given to purchasers and regulators but not the general public, and a sales stop for models exceeding 5% until corrective action and retest. S5 sets a mandatory recall at 12 incidents/100k with a corrective-action trigger at 8/100k, which is weaker than the discussed 8/100k recall trigger. S3 and S4 meet the red lines with a 6-year retrofit deadline and 36-month suppression deadline.
